newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Walter Matthau lets go of grumpy side - for now.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Walter Matthau lets go of grumpy side - for now.

text.p: Don't be fooled by his grumpy exterior. Walter Matthau has a soft side and he likes showing it -- sometimes.

Three years after starring in "Grumpy Old Men," and almost 20 years after originating the role of slob sportswriter Oscar Madison in "The Odd Couple," Matthau plays a romantic lead in his new movie, "The Grass Harp."

"I found it beautifully sad in spots and marvellously funny in other spots, but the crying stuck with me. I very rarely cry when I read something," Matthau told Reuters, referring to the script. But then, he adds with a chuckle, he lost a huge basketball bet the same day he read it.

Matthau, 75, plays Charlie Cool, a retired judge who joins a band of misfits living on the outskirts of a small Southern town. Despite years of isolation, Cool manages to summon up enough charm to attract a woman 20 years younger.

"He says lines like 'Love is a chain of love, as nature is a chain of life.' That's not exactly your typical Walter Matthau role," said Charles Matthau, the actor's son and director of the movie. It took the younger Matthau three years before he felt ready to show his father "The Grass Harp" screenplay, which he helped adapt.

"Usually you see him as the beer-drinking coach or the grumpy old man or the slob sportscaster," he said, referring to his father's roles in "The Bad News Bears," "The Odd Couple" and "Grumpy Old Men," movies that pigeonholed Matthau as a crank.

And audiences reacted to the latest film with surprise. When it premiered at the Toronto Film Festival, one person told Charles Matthau they would have "never thought of Walter Matthau for the part. They thought it was casting so much against type it was miscasting," the younger Matthau said.

But if Matthau's role is different, he is at least paired with a familiar cohort. Jack Lemmon, co-star of some of Matthau's biggest hits including "The Odd Couple" and "Grumpy Old Men," makes a brief appearance as Teflon-coated conman Morris Ritz.
Matthau said they work well together because their egos never come into play. "Also he's short and pretty, and I'm tall and homely."
He said he would rather not do the grumpy roles that have brought him recent success but admits it is hard landing work at his age. "How many 75-year-old guys are in the movies?"

But he can't complain too much. Along with "The Grass Harp," he will appear in "I'm Not Rappaport," a movie version of the Broodway play, due out in mid-November. Another instalment of "Grumpy Old Men" is also ready to shoot.
Asked about some of his younger co-stars, however, he canot help but sound a bit curmudgeonly.

"Modern actors sometimes annoy me because I don't know what they're saying," he said. "I think young people today don't care about whether they can be heard, whether their voice is pleasant, whether their activities are motivated by any logical impulse. They just go in there and the more unintelligible you become the greater your chance at being a success."
What about his young co-star in "The Grass Harp" -- Edward Furlong -- did he ask him to speak up? "I think I hit him with that statement once. He got it immediately," Matthau said.
As for young actors overall, Matthau paused when asked who he liked? "I would, your honour, respectfully decline on the grounds that it may incriminate me later on," he said.
